I believe that the text in line 249 should refer to Figure 2b not 2a and then on line 250, it is referring to 2a not 2b. If that is the
case, perhaps consider restructuring the figure so the map is on the left and the genome coverage vs read maps and
unrooted maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree reversed. Similarly, there are several places where Figure 2f is referred to
(e.g. lines 300, 302,) where I suspect the authors were intending to highlight Figure 2e. Because of the huge number of
subpanels and Supplementary Figures with subpanels, can the authors please double check that each and every cross
reference is correct. Also, I suggest that the panel layout reflects the order in the text - Figure 3e and 3f are only referenced
on line 461 while 3g on 429 and 3h on 448… I understand that some of this is just making them visually appealing and to
make the figures fit in the space, but with so many essential Supplementary Figures and subpanels, it makes it slightly more
difficult jumping back and forth between the text and the supplements.
As far as I can tell, Figure 2c is not referred to anywhere in the text. Nor is Figure 4f. Nor is Figure 4g. I may have missed
these, but I did not find them despite trying. Moreover, I did not check each and every cross reference; please ensure that
EACH of the figures and presented data are referenced, discussed, and analysed. If not… there are several instances where
the Supplementary Figures are covered by considerable amounts of text or even get their own sections (e.g. Supplementary
Figures 21, 23). I’d ask the authors to consider if there are places to rethink the figures or rearrange them to make space for
data that is essential to your story.
Please make sure that in the results section discussing the candidate genes associated with local adaptation, that all
references and data are cross referenced. Line 444 talks about expression analysis of DsRZ2 across “different tissues” but
as far as I can tell you haven’t discussed sampling different tissue types.
Please move the label the Y axes for Figure 4b from above to the more conventional next to the axis location.
There is a strange symbol on line 567 in the text describing allele frequency, please correct.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript by Huang et al., entitled “The Digitaria genomes reveal local adaption and herbicide resistance mediated by
introgression” presents an impressive dataset and array of analyses to study the genomic diversity, evolutionary history, and
adaptation to herbicides in a pressing agricultural weed, Digitaria sanguinalis, commonly known as crab grass. In producing
very high quality reference genomes for not only the focal species but its diploid progenitors, the authors provide a valuable
resource for systematically classifying Digitaria accessions in agricultural landscapes. The expansive analyses of an
equally impressive population genomic dataset include model based inference of demographic history, population structure,
introgression gene-environment association, bio-assays for herbicide tolerance and accompanying GWA— the analyses on
the genetic architecture of non-target site resistance are especially impressive and convincing. However, the motivation for
several of the analyses presented are difficult to follow, and the conclusions given throughout the manuscript seem to
overstep the results presented. Generally, some work to improve the flow of writing, including explicitly stating the
hypotheses being tested for each analysis, would help readability of this elaborate work.
Line 229-230, 233-234: It seems very tentative to suggest gene family expansions relate to herbicide resistance when this
analysis was at the genus level, and there is plenty of variation in herbicide use / resistance levels within and across
species. To claim this, one would want to compare lineages contrasting in a history of herbicide use to see if this result
stands up. Similarly, that UDPs/GTs are enriched on Chromosome 3, which happens to also have the highest TE density,
does not convincingly show that TEs have driven an adaptive expansion of this gene family.
Lines 348-349: It would be useful to provide more context to help the reader interpret these results in the main text - what
was the temporal scale of longitudinal surveillance? How many years were sampled? Were the same localities revisited?
Either way, I would want to make sure that geographic coordinates were controlled for when conclusions are made about
structure changing through time to be sure it's not just driven by differences in space.
Lines 384: The authors claim early on that there was evidence for pervasive introgression between sympatric populations,
but more context in how these tests were performed would really help with interpreting these results. Were these tests
between the diploid, tetraploid, and hexaploid populations? Was there more introgression in some directions compared to
others? The authors note there is evidence for introgression in 7 tests, but how many total populations were tested?
Line 389: the acronym PIG is used before it is defined
Line 393-398: It is hard to interpret these results in the absence of a well defined null expectation. I would like to see a test of
whether correlations between PSIG and geographic distance / environmental divergence are greater than expected from the
genome-wide background levels of divergence /population structure. The fact that environmental divergence did not remain
a significant predictor after accounting for geographic distance to me, suggests that this pattern is in part due to population
structure, as we know it to be strongly structured by geography. Therefore, I do not believe this is evidence for
adaptive/environment mediated introgression.
Line 417-419: As there has been work focused on these gene families in NTSR, it seems a bit like an over
simplification/cherry-picking to mention only these gene families when there are supposedly 3500 genes introgressed. I also
was not able to find details in the methods about how these tests were performed. Generally, I find these results to provide
weak evidence of environment-driven selection shaping introgression patterns, which is concluded in the final sentence. It
seems like overlaying this work with the GEA results in the next section would first be necessary to say this. This is done for
only one gene – DsRZ2, but I would like to see a more systematic comparison of introgression regions with respect to
introgressed regions to support this more general conclusion the authors make.
Line 436: Genomics islands typically refer to a debate centered around speciation and reproductive isolation, not adaptation.
A more standard contrast would be polygenic adaptation vs. selective sweeps.
Line 450: Can you provide some context for interpreting the lack of significant difference between the T and C haplotype?
Line 473-474: How do we interpret survival rate vs control efficacy? I’m not sure I understand the difference.
Line 497: There is no data presented to support the conclusion that resistance has evolved independently multiple times.
That resistance accessions were widespread could be the result of gene flow and recombination onto local backgrounds.
Line 505: Are any of the mutations non-synonymous? This sentence could also use grammatical edits, and the entire
manuscript should be carefully edited for similar grammatical errors.
Lines 516-518: The authors ignore dominance in this discussion - a single dominant mutation present on only one genome-
copy could confer resistance, even in a hexaploid, so this does not conclusively rule out target-site resistance mechanisms.
Line 523: I think in this case it would be more accurate to say gene amplification rather than expansions? I think that the
GWAS is done based on coverage, so it would be more descriptive/informative to you “assessed variation in coverage”
rather than copy number. To help with readability more generally, I think this section could be shortened given the lack of
evidence for resistance associated with copy number variation.
Line 553: What is a GWAS prioritized gene?
Line 565: Again, what was the source population of the fd peak at DsSOH1? Where do we think this haplotype came from?
How many tests gave such a result?
Line 572/589: DsSOH1 is one of the numerous (~40) NTSR-associated loci you have detected. Therefore it feels like an
overstatement to conclude that introgression is a driving force behind NTSR. Do any of the other loci show such a signal? Is
it beyond what you would expect compared to the frequency of introgression across the rest of the genome?
Line 595-598: Unclear how these two analyses relate to one another
Line 681-684: I do not follow this sentence for both conceptual and grammatical reasons.
Line 687: I do not think this novelty statement is necessary or true. Adaptive introgression of herbicide resistance has been
shown in Teosinte from Maize (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32989136/) and in numerous other systems in response to
pesticides more broadly.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Huang et al., entitled “The Digitaria genomes reveal local adaption
and herbicide resistance mediated by introgression” presents an impressive dataset
and array of analyses to study the genomic diversity, evolutionary history, and
adaptation to herbicides in a pressing agricultural weed, Digitaria sanguinalis,
commonly known as crab grass. In producing very high quality reference genomes for
not only the focal species but its diploid progenitors, the authors provide a valuable
resource for systematically classifying Digitaria accessions in agricultural landscapes.
The expansive analyses of an equally impressive population genomic dataset include
model based inference of demographic history, population structure, introgression
gene-environment association, bio-assays for herbicide tolerance and accompanying
GWA— the analyses on the genetic architecture of non-target site resistance are
especially impressive and convincing. However, the motivation for several of the
analyses presented are difficult to follow, and the conclusions given throughout the
manuscript seem to overstep the results presented. Generally, some work to improve
the flow of writing, including explicitly stating the hypotheses being tested for each
analysis, would help readability of this elaborate work.
Response:
We appreciate your positive comments and constructive suggestions, which are very
helpful for improving our manuscript.
Line 229-230, 233-234: It seems very tentative to suggest gene family expansions
relate to herbicide resistance when this analysis was at the genus level, and there is
plenty of variation in herbicide use / resistance levels within and across species. To
claim this, one would want to compare lineages contrasting in a history of herbicide
use to see if this result stands up. Similarly, that UDPs/GTs are enriched on
Chromosome 3, which happens to also have the highest TE density, does not
convincingly show that TEs have driven an adaptive expansion of this gene family.
Response:
Thank you for this insightful comment, and we sorry for the confusion caused by the
initial phrasing of this section. We have realized that the causal relationship expressed
here requires more robust evidence to verify. While the observed expansion of
herbicide-related gene families in Digitaria may have provided a genomic foundation
for adaptation under herbicide exposure, there is currently no direct evidence linking
this expansion to herbicide selection. To avoid overinterpretation, we have now
removed the statement in Results section “contributed to adaptation to herbicide
selection” and revised the manuscript as:
“These expansions may have provided a genomic foundation for adaptation under
modern weed management systems.”
Transposable elements (TEs) have been implicated in rapid plant adaptation through
their role in promoting gene copy number variation (Lisch, 2013). In our case, we
observed that Chr3 exhibits both the highest TE density and an enrichment of UDP-
glucuronosyl/glucosyl transferase (UDP/GT). While this co-localization may suggest
a possible association, we concur that the current evidence is insufficient to establish a
correlation between TE activity and the expansion of this gene family.
To avoid misunderstanding, we have now removed the statement in the Results

revised the manuscript as:

< 0.01) (Supplementary Fig. 10), which also harbors the highest transposon density

To detect genes underlying heritable phenotypic variation, both top-down approaches

analyses) and bottom-up approaches (e. g., population genomics) are commonly
employed. In this study, we adopted a bottom-up approach, extended haplotype

Line 473-474: How do we interpret survival rate vs control efficacy? I’m not sure I
understand the difference.
Response:
Survival rate (%) measures the proportion of individual plants that physically
“survived” the herbicide insult (binary dead / alive scoring). A survival rate of 100 %
means every plant stayed alive; 0 % means all plants were completely necrotic.
Control efficacy (%) quantifies how much total biomass was reduced by the treatment
relative to the non-treated control, irrespective of how many individuals lived or died.
An efficacy of 100 % indicates total biomass suppression (no living tissue), whereas
0 % means biomass was identical to the control.
Thus, the survival rate reflects the number of surviving plants, whereas control
efficacy reflects the amount of living tissue. A treatment could kill only half of the
plants (50 % survival) yet strongly stunt the survivors, giving a high control efficacy
(e. g., 85 %). We now explicitly state this distinction in the revised manuscript and
have added the explanatory sentences above to the Results section as follows:
“Survival rates (number alive after treatment) following herbicide treatment rose
from 36.5% in 2013 to 74.2% in 2023 (Supplementary Table 18), while the mean
herbicide control efficacy (proportion of tissue successfully controlled) concurrently
declined from 86.0% to 70.7%.”

Response:
We are sorry for the confusion. In this context, we intended to refer to genes
significantly associated with herbicide resistance identified by GWAS. We have
revised the corresponding statement in the manuscript for improved clarity, as
follows:
“A total of 40 resistance-associated SNPs (rSNPs) were identified, corresponding to
19 genes, including three homologs of genes functionally validated to confer non-
target-site herbicide resistance in other grass species (Fig. 4c) (Chen et al., 2025;
Goldberg-Cavalleri et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2022)”
Line 565: Again, what was the source population of the fd peak at DsSOH1? Where
do we think this haplotype came from? How many tests gave such a result?
Response:
We apologize for the lack of a clearly defined null expectation in our analysis of the
origin of DsSOH1, which may have contributed to ambiguity in the text.
To infer the potential origin of DsSOH1, we employed the ABBA-BABA test under
the topology (((P1, P2), P3), O), with D. bicornis as the outgroup (O), susceptible D.
sanguinalis as P1, resistant D. sanguinalis as P2, and D. ciliaris as P3
(Supplementary Fig. 31a). Regions introgressed from D. ciliaris into the resistant
group were expected to display elevated f values. The prominent f peak at the
d d
DsSOH1 locus thus suggests that D. ciliaris may have contributed alleles to this
region. This inference is further supported by the phylogenetic tree constructed from
the 100-kb regions surrounding DsSOH1, where the topology is consistent with
introgression from D. ciliaris (Fig. 4h).
However, since resistant accessions did not form a monophyletic clade, we
acknowledge that this pattern could alternatively be explained by independent
evolution or more complex gene flow events. We currently lack direct evidence to
distinguish these scenarios.
To assess whether different levels of resistance are associated with distinct patterns of
introgression, we conducted separate analyses for the Low Resistance (LR), Moderate
Resistance (MR), and High Resistance (HR) groups. Specifically, we included 10
accessions for HR, 43 for MR, 27 for LR, and 55 for the susceptible group in our
tests.
To clarify this issue, we have added a description of the null expectation in the revised
manuscript and provide a detailed representation of the null model in Supplementary
Fig. 32a.
“To trace the origin of the haplotype at DsSOH1, we applied ABBA-BABA analysis
using the topology (((P1, P2), P3), O), with D. bicornis, susceptible D. sanguinalis,
resistant D. sanguinalis, and D. ciliaris assigned to O, P1, P2, and P3, respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 32a). A prominent f peak was detected specifically within the
d
DsSOH1 locus in the HR group, implying potential introgression from D. ciliaris,
whereas the MR and LR groups exhibited progressively weaker admixture signals
(Fig. 4f).”
Line 572/589: DsSOH1 is one of the numerous (~40) NTSR-associated loci you have
detected. Therefore it feels like an overstatement to conclude that introgression is a
driving force behind NTSR. Do any of the other loci show such a signal? Is it beyond
what you would expect compared to the frequency of introgression across the rest of
the genome?
Response:
We agree that the introgression origin of DsSOH1, as one of the NTSR-associated
SNPs (rSNPs), is not sufficient to generalize introgression as the primary driving
force of NTSR.
To assess whether introgression broadly contributes to NTSR, we compared f values,
d
used here to quantify the strength of introgression from D. ciliaris, within 50-kb
windows surrounding rSNPs with those from genome-wide background regions. As
shown in Fig. R3, the HR group exhibited significantly elevated introgression
frequencies at rSNPs compared to the genomic background (Mann-Whitney U test, p
= 0.02). This pattern was not observed in the MR or LR groups.
Notably, the bimodal distribution of f values in the HR group suggests that while
d
introgression may contribute to herbicide resistance, it is unlikely to be the only
underlying mechanism.
Fig. R3 | Distribution of f values in LR, MR, and HR groups across 50-kb
d
windows surrounding rSNPs and genome-wide background regions. The dashed
line indicates the 90th percentile f value derived from the genomic background.
d
Statistical significance was assessed using a one-tailed Mann-Whitney U test.
Taken together, these results suggest a positive correlation between the frequency of
introgression from D. ciliaris and herbicide resistance levels in D. sanguinalis,
particularly in the most resistant populations. To avoid further misunderstanding, we
revised the statements at Line 572 as “Remarkably, the regions with the highest F
ST
differentiation between resistant and susceptible populations coincided precisely with
the f peak interval, strongly implicating introgression from D. ciliaris at the DsSOH1
d
locus (Fig. 4f).” and at Line 589 as “This recurrent phylogenetic pattern suggests
that the NTSR-associated resistant haplotype at DsSOH1 likely evolved through
parallel and recent introgression from neighboring D. ciliaris populations.”
We further present the association between introgression frequency from D. ciliaris
and herbicide resistance levels in D. sanguinalis in the next section.
Line 595-598: Unclear how these two analyses relate to one another
Response:
We appreciate your comment and agree that the relationship between the two analyses
was not clearly articulated in the original version. To improve clarity, we have revised
this section as follows:
“To investigate the correlation between introgression frequency from D. ciliaris and
herbicide resistance levels in D. sanguinalis, we compared the f values at rSNPs to
d
the genome-wide background. The HR group exhibited significantly higher
introgression frequencies at rSNPs compared to the genomic background (Mann-
Whitney U test, p = 0.02), a pattern not observed in the MR or LR groups
(Supplementary Fig. 31c). In addition, the HR group exhibited the greatest
cumulative length of introgressed windows across the genome (HR vs. MR, Mann-
Whitney U test, p = 1.6e-2; HR vs. LR, Mann-Whitney U test, p = 1.18e-4)
(Supplementary Fig. 31d). These findings suggest that introgression from D. ciliaris
may be associated with the development of NTSR in D. sanguinalis. Interestingly, we
observed an increase in the frequency of rSNPs in accessions collected in 2023
compared to those collected in 2013 (Supplementary Fig. 31e), which may be linked
to the higher herbicide resistance observed in 2023.”
Line 681-684: I do not follow this sentence for both conceptual and grammatical
reasons.
Response:
We agree that the original phrasing was grammatically problematic and conceptually
condensed. Our intention was to convey that introgression within the Digitaria
complex may contribute to local adaptation across diverse environments. We have
revised the sentence for clarity and precision as follows:
"Although introgression is increasingly recognized as a potential mechanism of
adaptive evolution, instances of beneficial introgression remain limited (Edelman et
al., 2019; Taylor and Larson, 2019). In our study, we identified recurrent post-
divergence introgression between D. ciliaris and D. sanguinalis, two species with
overlapping distributions across ecologically heterogeneous regions. This frequent
gene flow appears to have contributed to environmental adaptation in D. sanguinalis,
particularly with respect to cold tolerance (Fig. 3h). Similar patterns of adaptive
introgression have also been reported in oaks (Quercus spp.), where introgression
between sympatric species may contribute to climatic adaptation (Fu et al., 2022;
Ren et al., 2025). Given their widespread geographic overlap, such processes may be
prevalent within globally distributed weedy genera, such as Echinochloa
(barnyardgrass) and Setaria (green foxtail), where recurrent hybridization and
selection may drive local adaptation in response to heterogeneous environments
worldwide."
Line 687: I do not think this novelty statement is necessary or true. Adaptive
introgression of herbicide resistance has been shown in Teosinte from Maize
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32989136/) and in numerous other systems in
response to pesticides more broadly.
Response:
We sincerely apologize for the oversight in our literature citation and phrasing. We
fully acknowledge that adaptive introgression of herbicide resistance has been
previously reported, including the well-documented case of introgression from maize
to teosinte (Le Corre et al., 2020), as well as in other systems such as weedy rice
(Wedger et al., 2024, 2022) and Brassica (Pandolfo et al., 2016).
These studies have primarily focused on crop-to-weed gene flow. Our study highlights
a different scenario in which adaptive introgression occurs between two weedy
species within the Digitaria complex. This weed-to-weed gene flow may represent an
alternative and underappreciated route through which herbicide resistance can evolve
and spread. Furthermore, our study integrates extensive phenotypic screening of 196
representative accessions using dose-response assays, together with genome-wide
resequencing, allowing us to identify resistance-associated SNPs and provide genomic
evidence supporting their introgressive origin. We believe this combined approach
adds depth to the current understanding of how herbicide resistance can emerge via
interspecific introgression in weedy taxa.
We have revised the novelty statement to more accurately reflect the contribution of
this work within the context of existing literature, as follows:
“While introgression events in weeds have been increasingly documented (Ribeiro et
al., 2025; Wedger et al., 2024), our findings suggest that adaptive introgression
between closely related weedy species may contribute to the rapid evolution of
herbicide resistance.”

Le Corre, V., Siol, M., Vigouroux, Y., Tenaillon, M.I., Délye, C., 2020. Adaptive
introgression from maize has facilitated the establishment of teosinte as a noxious
weed in Europe. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 117, 25618–25627.
Wedger, M.J., Roma-Burgos, N., Olsen, K.M., 2022. Genomic revolution of US
weedy rice in response to 21st century agricultural technologies. Commun. Biol. 5,
885.
Wedger, M.J., Xiao, E., Butts, T.R., Chlapecka, J.L., Webster, L.C., Olsen, K.M.,
2024. Recent crop-to-weed adaptive introgression has reshaped the genomic
composition and geographical structure of US weedy rice (Oryza spp.). Mol. Ecol.
e17604.
Pandolfo, C.E., Presotto, A., Carbonell, F.T., Ureta, S., Poverene, M., Cantamutto, M.,
2016. Transgenic glyphosate-resistant oilseed rape (Brassica napus) as an invasive
weed in Argentina: detection, characterization, and control alternatives. Environ. Sci.
Pollut. Res. 23, 24081–24091.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This version of the manuscript still presents a very large and diverse dataset, including
phenotyping and then genome assembly and annotation of D. sanguinalis and its
progenitors, population genomics of 579 accessions (covering structure, diversity, and
demographic analyses), evidence of introgression and environmental adaptation,
herbicide resistance phenotyping with dose–response curves and spatiotemporal
trends, comparative analysis of target-site versus non-target-site resistance, GWAS for
NTSR loci, transcriptomic profiling of resistant versus susceptible biotypes, and
correlations between introgression and resistance. The manuscript’s discussion is
comparatively brief, focusing on evolutionary and management implications.
The manuscript is supported by extensive resources: 4 multipaneled figures, 38(?)
supplementary figures, 24 supplementary tables, 3 supplementary notes, and 4
supplementary datasets. Despite its complexity, the text is generally well-structured
and readable, though challenging for any single reviewer to evaluate in full given the
breadth of the science that is presented. The integrated approach provides a
comprehensive resource; I assume the authors have made a considered decision to
maintain this format rather than divide the work into separate papers.
I thank the authors for addressing many of my previous suggestions and for providing
a clear rebuttal outlining the changes made. Improvements include a more logical
introduction, smoother transitions, corrected terminology, revised abbreviations, and
clearer figure legends. These changes enhance readability and scientific clarity.
Areas for further attention:
Figure referencing: I pointed out previously that the figure references were incorrect
and sometimes the narrative did not match panel order. Because of the complexity of
the datasets and the edits that were made in the revision and time allocated to do the
revision, I have not systematically checked that the associations between text and
figures are all correct. I hope instead that authors have been more diligent in this
second revision and expect that this will be double checked in the production process
if the paper progresses.
Abstract: Now more comprehensive but still omits phenotyping, which according to
the text is novel and central to Figures 1a, 1c, and 2b.
Clarity: A few sentences remain unclear or incomplete. Please revisit these for
precision.
• 165 = “sequencing reads could be successfully mapped, with properly paired ____
(Supplementary Table 3).”
• 222 – 225 = “Flood-adapted genes, Echinochloa displayed marked expansion of …”
• 554 = “…collectively suggesting recent adaptive introgression through introgression…”
Clarity: Sentence at 553-554 “allele frequency around 0.4…” lacks the strange symbol that was in the previous version, but
what do you mean “around 0.4”? Is “around” equivalent to “approximately” and if so, why not simply use the appropriate
level of precision instead of stating “around”?
Interpretation: The text at lines 367-369 was rewritten to emphasize that interspecific
introgression events are more probable than hybridization and it now cites monocot
grafting incompatibility literature. Those additions, although useful do not explain the
rationale for introgression based on chloroplast phylogenies – perhaps because this is
not my speciality. Is introgression the only explanation for the observation? If so,
state this explicitly.
Interpretation: Although your data do not support a model of metabolic resistance mediated by gene amplification (lines 514-
515) do they exclude it? If not, please refine this sentence – lack of evidence is not evidence of lack. Particularly as you then
go on to explore NTSR mediated by e.g. CYP, AKR and ABC genes in the sections following line 532 and emphasize that
“NTSR has become the dominant resistance strategy” (line 644) in the Discussion – which remains quite brief compared to
the body of data presented.
Figures: Newly added figures (e.g., R1, R2, R3) appear strikingly similar to existing
supplementary figures. Please clarify whether these replace previous versions or
represent distinct data.
• How does the added figure Fig. R1 with the year by year collections differ from
what was already sent as Supplementary Figure 11? They seem to be the same except
that R1 is slightly more spaced out than Sup 11?
• The text at 430–431 now specifies root, stem, old leaf, young leaf; expression range
reported; Supp. Fig. 27a & Fig. R2 show profiles. However, how does Fig. R2 differ
from the data shown in Supplementary Fig. 27a except that now there are the three
datapoints indicated in R2? Are these the same data? If so, it is inappropriate to show
them twice. Will R2 replace Sup Fig 27a?
• Similarly, will R3 replace Supplementary Figure 32c? For all three of the
Supplementary Figures added in the revision, it is not clear how they differ from what
was already presented except perhaps minor cosmetic changes. Please explain.
Language: Some informal phrasing (e.g., “didn’t” at line 438) remains and should be
revised for scientific tone.
Minor Issues:

• The text at line 247 has CH, DH, and EH without subscripting.
• The authors alternate between using common names followed by bracketed Latin
names (e.g. “oaks (Quercus spp.”) on line 651 and then “Echinochloa (barnyardgrass) and Seteria (green foxtail)” on line 654). Choosing one way to state the
nomenclature or the other would make the manuscript more appropriate for the
scientific literature.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I appreciate the effort the authors put into reviewing this manuscript, updating the
conclusions to better reflect the analyses run and evidence provided. I maintain this is
an interesting manuscript full of useful data and insights to the field. In terms of
presentation, I do find this version easier to follow--however, there is still quite a lot
of room for improvement throughout. While I will give a few examples of recurring
communication issues, I encourage the authors to take a very careful look at the
spelling, grammar, and narrative arc throughout.
Communication Issues:
- Connection between subsections: When reading the manuscript, sections feel very
disjunct from each other, and only start to come together near the end and with the
synthesis in the discussion. If the authors could incorporate some more
transitional sentences throughout, and weave in why it was first important to understand
(for e.g.) demographic history & pop structure before studying introgression etc, it
would strengthen the cohesiveness of the paper. The same is true for paragraphs of the
introduction -- as written, they seem almost unrelated, although clearly that is not true.
- Motivation for analyses: not completely unrelated to the above point, but I still feel
there is opportunity to help the reader better understand the reasoning and progression
from analysis to analysis - given how many analyses the authors present, this is really
important. For e.g. in the Section on Resistance, the authors have subsections on the
temporal/spatial distribution of phenotypic resistance, TSR and NTSR variation, and
then Transcriptomic analysis. While experts in the field would intuit why all of these
were done, motivation should be given at the beginning of each section why and how
the authors expect these approaches to be informative about Resistance evolution.
Grammatical and spelling issues throughout: There remain numerous grammatical
errors that affect readability and professionalism. This is not an exhaustive list, but
examples include:
--> Title: "local adaption" should be "local adaptation"
-->Line 17 (Highlights): "Introgression from sympatric relatives have contributed" - subject-verb disagreement (should be
"has contributed")
-->Introduction: "Polyploidy is across the plant kingdom" - missing word (should be "Polyploidy is common across" or
"Polyploidy is found across")
-->Results, line ~50: "we significant lineage-specific contraction" - missing verb (should be "we observed significant")
-->Not a gramatical error but the section header “Population structure restructuration in ten years” reads very awkwardly.
-->Multiple instances of missing spaces after punctuation, incomplete sentences, and
words missing letters.
-->Some terminology is used inconsistently (e.g., "NTSR-associated SNPs" vs "resistance-associated SNPs" vs "rSNPs")
-->Please look to see where run-on sentences can be split for clarity.
- Figure legends: Several figure legends could be more informative and self-contained:
-->All abbreviations should be defined in each legend
-->Statistical tests used should be mentioned in the legend when significance is
indicated
-->The legends should allow readers to understand the main takeaway without having
to refer back to the main text
- Data availability: While the authors mention data will be made available, specific
details are still missing:
-->Accession numbers for genome assemblies
-->Repository information for resequencing data
-->Code availability for custom analyses should be included in a Data Availability
statement.

showed marked expansion in Echinochloa (copy number: 182.0 ± 12.3 vs. 159.0 ± 9.9

introgression…”
Response:
We have revised it for clarity and to avoid repetition. The sentence now reads:
“Notably, the DsSOH1 variant was not fixed in HR group, with an observed allele
frequency of 0.40, supporting a scenario of recent adaptive introgression (Fig. 4d).”
Clarity: Sentence at 553-554 “allele frequency around 0.4…” lacks the strange
symbol that was in the previous version, but what do you mean “around 0.4”? Is
“around” equivalent to “approximately” and if so, why not simply use the appropriate
level of precision instead of stating “around”?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion and have now revised the sentence
to improve clarity and precision. Specifically, we replaced “around 0.4” with the exact
value “0.40” (as calculated from the genotype calls). The revised sentence reads:
“Notably, the DsSOH1 variant was not fixed in HR group, with an observed allele
frequency of 0.40, supporting a scenario of recent adaptive introgression (Fig. 4d).”
Interpretation: The text at lines 367-369 was rewritten to emphasize that interspecific
introgression events are more probable than hybridization and it now cites monocot
grafting incompatibility literature. Those additions, although useful do not explain the
rationale for introgression based on chloroplast phylogenies – perhaps because this is
not my speciality. Is introgression the only explanation for the observation? If so,
state this explicitly.
Response:
We apologize for the confusion. In light of the chloroplast phylogenies, interspecific
introgression remains the most plausible and well-supported explanation for the
observed patterns. While alternative possibilities such as incomplete lineage sorting or
sample misidentification were considered, these are less consistent with the combined
evidence from bootstrap support, nuclear-chloroplast discordance, and morphological
characters. We also acknowledge the theoretical possibility of natural grafting as a
source of chloroplast capture; however, this phenomenon is extremely rare in
monocots, especially grasses. Therefore, interspecific introgression-likely mediated
by historical hybridization events-is the most likely explanation, as has been similarly
demonstrated in genera such as Secale and Malus (Liu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022).
We have revised the text in the manuscript accordingly to state this interpretation
more clearly.
“Overall, the chloroplast phylogenies indicate extensive interspecific introgression
across Digitaria, most likely resulting from historical hybridization events (Feng et
al., 2024; Gaut et al., 2019).”
