### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Huang et al., entitled “The Digitaria genomes reveal local adaption and herbicide resistance mediated by
introgression” presents an impressive dataset and array of analyses to study the genomic diversity, evolutionary history, and
adaptation to herbicides in a pressing agricultural weed, Digitaria sanguinalis, commonly known as crab grass. In producing
very high quality reference genomes for not only the focal species but its diploid progenitors, the authors provide a valuable
resource for systematically classifying Digitaria accessions in agricultural landscapes. The expansive analyses of an
equally impressive population genomic dataset include model based inference of demographic history, population structure,
introgression gene-environment association, bio-assays for herbicide tolerance and accompanying GWA— the analyses on
the genetic architecture of non-target site resistance are especially impressive and convincing. However, the motivation for
several of the analyses presented are difficult to follow, and the conclusions given throughout the manuscript seem to
overstep the results presented. Generally, some work to improve the flow of writing, including explicitly stating the
hypotheses being tested for each analysis, would help readability of this elaborate work.
Line 229-230, 233-234: It seems very tentative to suggest gene family expansions relate to herbicide resistance when this
analysis was at the genus level, and there is plenty of variation in herbicide use / resistance levels within and across
species. To claim this, one would want to compare lineages contrasting in a history of herbicide use to see if this result
stands up. Similarly, that UDPs/GTs are enriched on Chromosome 3, which happens to also have the highest TE density,
does not convincingly show that TEs have driven an adaptive expansion of this gene family.
Lines 348-349: It would be useful to provide more context to help the reader interpret these results in the main text - what
was the temporal scale of longitudinal surveillance? How many years were sampled? Were the same localities revisited?
Either way, I would want to make sure that geographic coordinates were controlled for when conclusions are made about
structure changing through time to be sure it's not just driven by differences in space.
Lines 384: The authors claim early on that there was evidence for pervasive introgression between sympatric populations,
but more context in how these tests were performed would really help with interpreting these results. Were these tests
between the diploid, tetraploid, and hexaploid populations? Was there more introgression in some directions compared to
others? The authors note there is evidence for introgression in 7 tests, but how many total populations were tested?
Line 389: the acronym PIG is used before it is defined
Line 393-398: It is hard to interpret these results in the absence of a well defined null expectation. I would like to see a test of
whether correlations between PSIG and geographic distance / environmental divergence are greater than expected from the
genome-wide background levels of divergence /population structure. The fact that environmental divergence did not remain
a significant predictor after accounting for geographic distance to me, suggests that this pattern is in part due to population
structure, as we know it to be strongly structured by geography. Therefore, I do not believe this is evidence for
adaptive/environment mediated introgression.
Line 417-419: As there has been work focused on these gene families in NTSR, it seems a bit like an over
simplification/cherry-picking to mention only these gene families when there are supposedly 3500 genes introgressed. I also
was not able to find details in the methods about how these tests were performed. Generally, I find these results to provide
weak evidence of environment-driven selection shaping introgression patterns, which is concluded in the final sentence. It
seems like overlaying this work with the GEA results in the next section would first be necessary to say this. This is done for
only one gene – DsRZ2, but I would like to see a more systematic comparison of introgression regions with respect to
introgressed regions to support this more general conclusion the authors make.
Line 436: Genomics islands typically refer to a debate centered around speciation and reproductive isolation, not adaptation.
A more standard contrast would be polygenic adaptation vs. selective sweeps.
Line 450: Can you provide some context for interpreting the lack of significant difference between the T and C haplotype?
Line 473-474: How do we interpret survival rate vs control efficacy? I’m not sure I understand the difference.
Line 497: There is no data presented to support the conclusion that resistance has evolved independently multiple times.
That resistance accessions were widespread could be the result of gene flow and recombination onto local backgrounds.
Line 505: Are any of the mutations non-synonymous? This sentence could also use grammatical edits, and the entire
manuscript should be carefully edited for similar grammatical errors.
Lines 516-518: The authors ignore dominance in this discussion - a single dominant mutation present on only one genome-
copy could confer resistance, even in a hexaploid, so this does not conclusively rule out target-site resistance mechanisms.
Line 523: I think in this case it would be more accurate to say gene amplification rather than expansions? I think that the
GWAS is done based on coverage, so it would be more descriptive/informative to you “assessed variation in coverage”
rather than copy number. To help with readability more generally, I think this section could be shortened given the lack of
evidence for resistance associated with copy number variation.
Line 553: What is a GWAS prioritized gene?
Line 565: Again, what was the source population of the fd peak at DsSOH1? Where do we think this haplotype came from?
How many tests gave such a result?
Line 572/589: DsSOH1 is one of the numerous (~40) NTSR-associated loci you have detected. Therefore it feels like an
overstatement to conclude that introgression is a driving force behind NTSR. Do any of the other loci show such a signal? Is
it beyond what you would expect compared to the frequency of introgression across the rest of the genome?
Line 595-598: Unclear how these two analyses relate to one another
Line 681-684: I do not follow this sentence for both conceptual and grammatical reasons.
Line 687: I do not think this novelty statement is necessary or true. Adaptive introgression of herbicide resistance has been
shown in Teosinte from Maize (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32989136/) and in numerous other systems in response to
pesticides more broadly.

Response:
Sorry for the confusion caused by the lack of clarity. In this section, our intention was
to integrate nuclear and plastid phylogenies to propose preliminary hypotheses
regarding the reticulate evolutionary history of Digitaria. Either sexual hybridization
or asexual grafting can lead to chloroplast capture or horizontal transfer (Bock, 2010).
However, monocots are generally considered graft-incompatible due to the absence of
a vascular cambium and the dispersed arrangement of their vascular bundles (Feng et
al., 2024; Gaut et al., 2019; Melnyk and Meyerowitz, 2015). Thus, the observed
cytonuclear discordance is more plausibly explained by post-speciation hybridization.
We have revised the relevant text to better highlight the inference of widespread
hybridization events in Digitaria and to improve semantic clarity.
“Overall, the chloroplast phylogenies indicate extensive interspecific introgression
across Digitaria, likely driven by historical hybridization events, given the
improbability of natural grafting in grasses (Feng et al., 2024; Gaut et al., 2019).”

The manuscript by Huang et al., entitled “The Digitaria genomes reveal local adaption

Line 473-474: How do we interpret survival rate vs control efficacy? I’m not sure I
understand the difference.
Response:
Survival rate (%) measures the proportion of individual plants that physically
“survived” the herbicide insult (binary dead / alive scoring). A survival rate of 100 %
means every plant stayed alive; 0 % means all plants were completely necrotic.
Control efficacy (%) quantifies how much total biomass was reduced by the treatment
relative to the non-treated control, irrespective of how many individuals lived or died.
An efficacy of 100 % indicates total biomass suppression (no living tissue), whereas
0 % means biomass was identical to the control.
Thus, the survival rate reflects the number of surviving plants, whereas control
efficacy reflects the amount of living tissue. A treatment could kill only half of the
plants (50 % survival) yet strongly stunt the survivors, giving a high control efficacy
(e. g., 85 %). We now explicitly state this distinction in the revised manuscript and
have added the explanatory sentences above to the Results section as follows:
“Survival rates (number alive after treatment) following herbicide treatment rose
from 36.5% in 2013 to 74.2% in 2023 (Supplementary Table 18), while the mean
herbicide control efficacy (proportion of tissue successfully controlled) concurrently
declined from 86.0% to 70.7%.”

to teosinte (Le Corre et al., 2020), as well as in other systems such as weedy rice
(Wedger et al., 2024, 2022) and Brassica (Pandolfo et al., 2016).
These studies have primarily focused on crop-to-weed gene flow. Our study highlights
a different scenario in which adaptive introgression occurs between two weedy
species within the Digitaria complex. This weed-to-weed gene flow may represent an
alternative and underappreciated route through which herbicide resistance can evolve
and spread. Furthermore, our study integrates extensive phenotypic screening of 196
representative accessions using dose-response assays, together with genome-wide
resequencing, allowing us to identify resistance-associated SNPs and provide genomic
evidence supporting their introgressive origin. We believe this combined approach
adds depth to the current understanding of how herbicide resistance can emerge via
interspecific introgression in weedy taxa.
We have revised the novelty statement to more accurately reflect the contribution of
this work within the context of existing literature, as follows:
“While introgression events in weeds have been increasingly documented (Ribeiro et
al., 2025; Wedger et al., 2024), our findings suggest that adaptive introgression
between closely related weedy species may contribute to the rapid evolution of
herbicide resistance.”
